questions.prompt: Define an isomorphism between real vector spaces.
questions.answer: An isomorphism is a linear map that is both one-to-one and onto. Equivalently, it is a linear map with a linear inverse. If there is an isomorphism from V to W, then V and W have the same linear structure.

questions.prompt: Are \(\mathbb R^3\) and \(P_2\) isomorphic as real vector spaces? Explain.
questions.answer: Yes. \(\mathbb R^3\) has dimension 3, and \(P_2\) has basis \(\{1,x,x^2\}\), so \(\dim(P_2)=3\). Finite-dimensional real vector spaces with the same dimension are isomorphic. One isomorphism is \((a,b,c)\mapsto a+bx+cx^2\).

questions.prompt: Are \(\mathbb R^2\) and \(P_2\) isomorphic as real vector spaces? Explain.
questions.answer: No. \(\mathbb R^2\) has dimension 2, while \(P_2\) has dimension 3. Finite-dimensional real vector spaces are isomorphic only if they have the same dimension. Therefore \(\mathbb R^2\) and \(P_2\) are not isomorphic.

questions.prompt: Show that \(T:P_2 \to \mathbb R^3\) defined by \(T(a+bx+cx^2)=(a,b,c)\) is an isomorphism.
questions.answer: The map is linear because coefficients of sums and scalar multiples behave componentwise. It is one-to-one because \(T(a+bx+cx^2)=(0,0,0)\) implies \(a=b=c=0\), so the polynomial is zero. It is onto because every \((a,b,c)\) in \(\mathbb R^3\) is the image of \(a+bx+cx^2\). Therefore \(T\) is an isomorphism.

questions.prompt: When is a matrix map \(T(x)\) = Ax from \(\mathbb R^n\) to \(\mathbb R^n\) an isomorphism?
questions.answer: The map is an isomorphism exactly when A is invertible. If A is invertible, then T has inverse \(y\mapsto A^{-1}y\), so T is one-to-one and onto. If A is not invertible, then the map fails to be one-to-one or onto.

No. Although \(D\) maps onto \(P_2\), it is not one-to-one because every constant polynomial has derivative zero. The kernel is \(\operatorname{span}(1)\), not just \(\{0\}\). Since an isomorphism must be one-to-one and onto, \(D\) is not an isomorphism.

No. The domain \(P_2\) has dimension 3, while the codomain \(P_1\) has dimension 2. Vector spaces of different finite dimensions cannot be isomorphic. Also, \(D\) has non-zero constants in its kernel, so it is not one-to-one.

questions.prompt: Give an isomorphism from \(M_{2,2}(\mathbb R)\) to \(\mathbb R^4\).
questions.answer: One isomorphism sends a matrix to its entries in order: \(T(\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix})=(a,b,c,d)\). This map is linear because matrix addition and scalar multiplication act entry by entry. It is one-to-one and onto because each 4-tuple corresponds to exactly one \(2\times 2\) matrix.

questions.prompt: If \(T:V\to W\) is an isomorphism and \(\dim(V)=5\), what is \(\dim(W)\)?
questions.answer: An isomorphism preserves dimension. Since \(T\) is an isomorphism from \(V\) to \(W\) and \(\dim(V)=5\), it follows that \(\dim(W)=5\).

questions.prompt: A learner says two spaces are isomorphic only if their elements look the same. Diagnose the error.
questions.answer: Isomorphism means the spaces have the same linear structure, not that their elements look identical. For example, \(P_2\) and \(\mathbb R^3\) are isomorphic because both have dimension 3, even though one contains polynomials and the other contains coordinate triples. The learner is confusing representation with structure.
